question:
Patient note:
An 86-year-old man who spent nearly half a century maintaining diesel locomotives for the state rail line arrived to the pre-operative consultation this morning walking slowly but unassisted, carrying a thin folder that contained outside imaging reports and a neatly handwritten medication list. Over the past year he has noted a gradually intensifying morning cough productive of scant white sputum, occasional wheeze while climbing the single flight to his apartment, and two winter flare-ups that required five-day prednisone tapers from his primary physician but never emergency-department evaluation or ventilatory support. Baseline spirometry performed last month for surgical planning recorded an FEV1 of 1.05 L (55 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.45 and less than 6 % reversibility after 400 µg salbutamol; a postero-anterior chest radiograph the same day showed hyperinflated lung fields and flattened diaphragms but no infiltrates. He inhales tiotropium 18 µg each dawn and budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg two puffs twice daily, empties an albuterol inhaler roughly every six weeks when neighborhood sidewalks become steep, and saturates 95 % on ambient air at rest today with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min. A screening low-dose CT obtained for lung-cancer surveillance six months ago incidentally revealed a 2.1 cm spiculated lesion in the right upper lobe; subsequent PET–CT demonstrated avid uptake confined to that nodule without mediastinal, hepatic, adrenal, or osseous activity, and bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated non-small-cell carcinoma. Cardiothoracic colleagues plan a video-assisted thoracoscopic lobectomy and have requested clearance in view of his advanced age and pulmonary limitations. 

The patient denies ever experiencing crushing retrosternal pressure, diaphoresis with exertion, unexpected dyspnea when lying flat, awakening suddenly gasping, or bilateral ankle swelling, and he has never been hospitalized for a myocardial infarction. He walks four short city blocks at his own pace to the grocery and pauses only for breathlessness related to his chronic airway disease rather than calf discomfort, and he has never undergone lower-extremity bypass, angioplasty, or evaluation for claudication. He has no history of connective-tissue or autoimmune disorders, peptic ulcer disease, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Neurologically he recalls no episodes of facial droop, unilateral weakness, transient speech disturbance, visual blackout, seizure, or memory lapses; he still balances his checkbook without errors and recounts the dates of his grandchildren’s birthdays from memory. Routine HIV screening performed three years ago was negative, and he has never had opportunistic infections. Serial complete blood counts have remained within normal ranges, and he has no personal history of hematologic malignancy. 

His past laboratory panels have shown mildly elevated transaminases attributed to a combination of long-standing statin therapy and hepatic steatosis documented by ultrasound three months ago, which revealed a homogeneous hyperechoic liver measuring 15 cm with smooth contour, patent portal flow, and no splenomegaly. At that draw alanine aminotransferase was 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 84 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1; he has never developed jaundice, abdominal distention, encephalopathy, or required diuretics. Fasting plasma glucose recorded during last week’s comprehensive metabolic panel was 102 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.6 %, values he maintains with portion control and evening walks—he takes no hypoglycemic agents and logs carbohydrate intake on paper. Renal indices today include sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 78 mL/min/1.73 m²; urinalysis is bland with no protein, blood, or casts. Lipid profile last month demonstrated total cholesterol 208 mg/dL, LDL 118 mg/dL, HDL 46 mg/dL, and triglycerides 130 mg/dL; he takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly without myalgias. Current medications also include low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg each morning for systolic pressures that average 130s mm Hg at home, and cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily; he reports no drug allergies. He quit cigarettes 18 years ago after accumulating 55 pack-years, drinks a single glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is remarkable for a brother who died from pneumonia at 90 and a father who succumbed to “old age” at 93; there are no early strokes, coronary interventions, peripheral amputations, or cirrhotic complications among first-degree relatives. 

Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight loss beyond four pounds since the biopsy, hemoptysis, chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, abdominal pain, hematemesis, melena, dysuria, gross hematuria, or rash. On examination he appears lean and attentive, seated comfortably. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate as noted, weight 69 kg, height 173 cm, and body-mass index 23 kg/m². Oral mucosa is moist without cyanosis. Neck is supple, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation rises to 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung percussion is hyperresonant bilaterally, and auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds with scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. The abdomen is flat and nontender; the liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, smooth and mildly tender to deep inspiration, with no shifting dullness. Extremities are warm with 2+ radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses, capillary refill under two seconds, no digital clubbing, cyanosis, or edema. Neurologic screen shows orientation to person, place, and date, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady gait albeit slowed by mild exertional dyspnea. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, axis within normal limits, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, and no pathologic Q waves or ST-segment deviation. 

The surgical team seeks guidance regarding peri-operative inhaler scheduling, need for pre-habilitation to enhance postoperative pulmonary mechanics, interpretation of his mildly abnormal liver enzymes in the context of anticipated anesthesia, and recommendations for antiplatelet management around the planned minimally invasive resection.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adds age points to weighted chronic disease points.
- Age: 50–59 years scores 1, 60–69 scores 2, 70–79 scores 3, and ≥80 scores 4. At 86, he scores 4.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: symptomatic COPD with persistent airflow obstruction (+1).
- Mild liver disease: documented fatty liver with elevated transaminases, preserved synthetic function, and no portal hypertension (+1).
- Solid tumor: active, biopsy-confirmed lung cancer confined to the lung, so use the nonmetastatic tumor weight (+2), not the metastatic weight (+6).
- Other CCI conditions: no documented MI, heart failure, peripheral vascular or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, paralysis, connective-tissue disease, peptic ulcer, diabetes, moderate/severe renal disease, leukemia, lymphoma, or AIDS (+0 each).
Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8.
Final answer: 8
